summary: This Wikipedia-derived note surveys the Republic of the Marshall Islands: its government structure, religious makeup, energy and climate challenges, population and emigration, and a long history from early Micronesian settlement through European naming, German and Japanese control, and American occupation in World War II. It also covers the country's UN admission in 1991, its Compact of Free Association with the United States, and its geography of atolls split into Ratak and Ralik chains.
one_line: Overview of the Marshall Islands covering government, religion, energy, climate risks, population, geography, and history from settlement through UN membership.
key_facts: Legislative power lies with the Nitijela, and the upper house, the Council of Iroij, is an advisory body of twelve tribal chiefs.
The Presidential Cabinet consists of ten ministers appointed by the President with the approval of the Nitijela.
The country is divided into twenty-four electoral districts that correspond to the inhabited islands and atolls.
The United Church of Christ (formerly Congregational) has 51.5% of the population, and the Assemblies of God has 24.2%.
In 2007, the Marshall Islands joined the International Labour Organization.
A 57 kW solar power plant installed in 2009 was the largest in the Pacific at the time, including New Zealand.
In 2013, a drought left 6,000 people surviving on less than 1 litre of water per day in the northern atolls.
The Marshall Islands was admitted to the United Nations on September 17, 1991, through General Assembly Resolution 46/3.
In July 2011, the number of island residents was estimated at about 72,191.
About 4,300 Marshall Islanders have relocated to Springdale, Arkansas, the largest population concentration of natives outside their island home.
The islands were named for Captain John Charles Marshall on Western charts, while natives historically called their home "jolet jen Anij" (Gifts from God).
In 1944, during the Gilbert and Marshall Islands campaign, Americans captured Kwajalein Atoll, Majuro and Enewetak within one month.
The Compact of Free Association gives the United States sole responsibility for international defense of the Marshall Islands.
The Marshall Islands claims Wake Island, which the Marshallese government calls Enen-kio and the United States has administered since 1899.
The country consists of 29 atolls and five isolated islands with about 70 square miles of land across about 750,000 square miles of ocean.
On June 28, 1919, Germany signed the Treaty of Versailles under protest, renouncing its Pacific possessions including the Marshall Islands.
